body.hook: Some actors are almost unrecognizable from role to role: they change how they walk, stand, breathe and gesture. That transformation starts in the body. Rudolf Laban, a movement theorist, gave actors a vocabulary for describing how people move, and it's still used in drama schools around the world.

vocabulary.definition: How an actor uses their body to create a character.
Eight types of movement described by weight, time and space.
In Laban, whether movement is strong (heavy) or light.
In Laban, whether movement is sudden or sustained.
In Laban, whether movement is direct or indirect (flexible).
The part of the body a character seems to lead with, such as the chest, head or hips.

study.title: Moving as Someone Else
study.question: How do actors transform physically for a role?
study.passage:
Laban's eight efforts combine weight, time and space:
• Punch: strong, sudden, direct
• Press: strong, sustained, direct
• Slash: strong, sudden, indirect
• Wring: strong, sustained, indirect
• Dab: light, sudden, direct
• Glide: light, sustained, direct
• Flick: light, sudden, indirect
• Float: light, sustained, indirect
Part 1, Explore (15 minutes): Move around the room in each effort, starting with the hands, then the whole body, then walking. Notice how each makes you feel.
Part 2, Leading centres (10 minutes): Walk leading with the nose, then the chest, the hips, the knees. What kind of person does each suggest?
Part 3, Build a character (20 minutes): Choose a character from a play you're studying (or invent one). Decide: dominant effort, leading centre, tempo, and one signature gesture. Perform a 1-minute silent scene: the character enters a room, waits for someone who doesn't arrive, and leaves.
Audience feedback: What did they learn about the character without words?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; Laban efforts are from Rudolf Laban's movement analysis.
discussion: Which effort felt most unlike you, and why?
What did leading with the chest suggest about a person?
What did the audience learn about your character without words?
How could your character's effort change during a play?
study.product: Write a physicality profile for a character: dominant Laban effort, leading centre, tempo, posture and signature gesture, with reasons from the script or your character concept.

practice.q: What three factors make up Laban efforts?

practice.a: The body part a character leads with.

practice.q: What happens in the silent scene?
practice.a: A character enters, waits for someone who doesn't arrive and leaves.
A repeated movement that defines a character.

practice.q: Why do actors build physicality before lines?
practice.a: The body shapes how lines are spoken and how the character feels.

practice.q: How can an effort show a character's emotion?
practice.a: Sudden, strong efforts can show anger; light, sustained ones calm.

practice.q: Why is a silent scene a good test of physicality?
practice.a: The audience must read the character only from movement.

practice.q: How might two characters' efforts create conflict on stage?
practice.a: Contrasting efforts, like punch and float, show opposing personalities.
